implementation_notes: C++20 makes the pattern the standard library's own notation: a range is piped through std::views::filter, std::views::transform, std::views::take and friends with the | operator, and the resulting view evaluates lazily as it is iterated - the working draft says range adaptors 'can be chained to create pipelines of range transformations that evaluate lazily as the resulting view is iterated'. That replaces the classic loop or std::transform-into-back_inserter structure with a non-owning, composable value. Materialise deliberately (std::ranges::to in C++23, or ranges::copy/for_each) when the result must be reused; keep the classic algorithm form when the project pins C++17 or when the chain must be stepped through in a debugger.
pitfalls: Views are non-owning and lazy: everything captured by reference (a temporary container, a local, a dangling range) must outlive the view, and each dereference re-invokes the transform.
filter_view::begin() caches its first iterator, so it is not const-qualified and a view reused after the underlying range changed can hand out a stale begin.
Iterating a view twice re-runs the predicates and transforms; materialise with std::ranges::to (C++23) if the result is traversed more than once or the transform has side effects.

variants.name: Pre-C++20 algorithms with output iterators
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++20 the same computation is written with the algorithms in <algorithm> and <numeric>: std::copy_if fills a filtered container through a std::back_inserter, std::transform maps, std::accumulate (or the parallel std::reduce) terminates the chain, and every call is eager and materialises its own output container. This replaces hand-written index loops and is the right choice on a C++11/14/17 codebase, or when the intermediate collections are wanted for inspection; prefer it also when a single fused loop measures faster than the chain of algorithm calls.
pitfalls: Every algorithm is eager: two stages mean two containers and two passes, so the chain pays allocations the C++20 view form avoids.
Output iterators must match the container: std::back_inserter does not work for std::set/std::map (they need std::inserter), and writing past a fixed-size output range is undefined behaviour.
